ABSTRACT Niemann‐Pick disease type C (NPC) is a rare neurodegenerative disease primarily caused by mutations in the NPC1 gene, which is associated with cholesterol trafficking impairment, and disruption of endolysosomal processing and extracellular vesicles (EVs). Here, for patients with NPC1 mutations (NPC) and age‐matched controls (CTL) we describe the EV profile of dermal fibroblasts ( n = 5 NPC, n = 3 CTL) and, for the first time, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF, n = 5 NPC, n = 5 CTL). EVs were enriched using size‐exclusion chromatography and characterized by immunoblot, transmission electron microscopy, and microchip resistive pulse sensing. Single vesicle flow cytometry showed increased EV concentration in NPC CSF versus CTLs. In fibroblasts, EV concentration inversely correlated with NPC1 protein levels that was partially attenuated by hydroxypropyl‐β‐cyclodextrin, an experimental NPC therapeutic. Direct stochastic imaging and multiplexed EV immunoassays revealed that NPC EVs were enriched for endolysosomal proteins (CD63, Lamp1). Three miRNAs (miR‐365‐3p, ‐654‐3p, ‐598‐3p) were increased in NPC fibroblast EVs and two (miR‐320a, ‐199a/b‐3p) in NPC CSF EVs. Pathway analysis using those miRNAs identified relevant diseases and functions (cell death and survival, molecular transport, heredity neurological disease). These results demonstrate that NPC1 gene mutations alter EV biogenesis and disease‐associated changes in cargo that may serve as clinical biomarkers or therapeutic targets for NPC, a devastating disease without a cure. cerebrospinal fluid dermal fibroblast cells extracellular vesicle lysosomal storage disorder microRNA Niemann‐Pick disease type C NPC1 National Instititutes of Health R01AG079356 T32AG055378 3.3 Enrichment of EVs From Human CSF and Patient‐Derived Dermal Fibroblasts In keeping with recommendations from the International Society of Extracellular Vesicles (ISEV) and its Cell Culture and CSF task forces (Thery et al. 2018 ; Welsh et al. 2024 ; Shekari et al. 2023 ; Sandau et al. 2024 ), we first validated methods to enrich EVs from patient CSF and fibroblast conditioned media. For fibroblasts, conditioned media was concentrated and SEC used to separate EV‐rich fractions from other media components ( Figure 2A ). Immunoblot confirmed that SEC fractions 1–4 were enriched for EV proteins (Flotillin‐1, CD63, and CD81) with depletion of bulk proteins (total protein stain) ( Figure 2B ). When pooled, fractions 1–4 showed enrichment for these EV proteins but not cytosolic cell protein GM130 ( Figure 2C ). MRPS showed that fibroblast EV preparations contained ∼1.3 × 10 9 particles/mL with a mean size of 78.9 nm ( Figure 2D ). Our CSF EV enrichment protocols were based on our previous publications (Sandau et al. 2022 ) and guidelines created by ISEV and its CSF Task Force (Thery et al. 2018 ; Welsh et al. 2024 ; Sandau et al. 2024a ; Sandau et al. 2024b ). We used ultrafiltration to concentrate CSF followed by SEC to separate EVs from other CSF content, such as proteins and lipoproteins ( Figure 3A ). Immunoblots confirmed that SEC fractions 3–5 were enriched for the EV proteins Flotillin‐1 and CD81 with low levels of Albumin, a non‐EV protein that is abundant in CSF ( Figure 3B ). When pooled, fractions 3–5 again showed high levels of EV proteins Flotillin‐1 and CD81 and low levels of albumin and the lipoprotein ApoA1 ( Figure 3C ). MRPS demonstrated that CSF EV preparations contained ∼2.1 × 10 8 particles/mL with a mean size of 70 nm ( Figure 3D ). In agreement, TEM showed the presence of lipid‐enclosed particles of ∼100 nm ( Figure 3E , black arrows) as well as smaller particles around 50 nm ( Figure 3E , white arrows). Given the high input volumes required for CSF SEC, we also explored alternative enrichment methods for downstream single particle analysis by VFC and dSTORM ( Table S1 ). Using ultrafiltration, we found that concentrating CSF ten‐fold (10x CSF) increased particle yield over SEC‐based isolations without altering particle size ( Figure S10) . 3.4 NPC1 Fibroblast and CSF EVs Are Enriched in Disease‐Relevant miRNAs Previous research has shown that miRNA expression is altered in NPC, including spleen and liver tissue from NPC1 knockout mice and dermal fibroblasts from a single NPC1 patient (Ozsait et al. 2010 ; Pergande et al. 2019 ). We and others have demonstrated that EV miRNA content is also influenced by disease state (Sandau et al. 2022 ; Sandau et al. 2020 ; Das et al. 2019 ), yet nothing is yet known about the impact of NPC1 dysfunction on miRNA expression in EVs. We thus sought to determine the miRNA profiles of our samples and began by establishing miRNA expression in the fibroblast cell lines. Of 377 human miRNAs we assayed, 178 were expressed in cells ( Figure 4A , Table S3D ). Three miRNAs were significantly upregulated (FDR corrected threshold p < 0.004) by at least 1.5‐fold in NPC fibroblasts relative to CTL fibroblasts: 365‐3a/b‐3p, 654‐3p, and 598‐3p ( Figure 4B– D ). Five additional miRNAs were upregulated (652‐3p, 493‐3p, 134–5p, 127‐3p) or downregulated (34c‐5p) by at least 1.5‐fold with p < 0.05 but were not considered statistically significant based on the FDR ( Figure 4A , pink dots). Interestingly, expression of the three significantly upregulated miRNAs inversely correlated with cellular NPC1 expression ( Figure 4E– G ), as measured by immunoblot ( Figure 1A ). To better understand the potential impact of these miRNAs, we next explored the biological functions and diseases they may operate in. We used the publicly available database miRTarbase (Huang et al. 2022 ) to identify experimentally validated mRNA targets of miR‐365‐3p, ‐654‐3p, and ‐598‐3p, as well as TargetScan (Agarwal et al. 2015 ) and miRDB (Chen and Wang, 2020 ) to identify predicted mRNA targets. Together, these tools identified 935 mRNA targets, which were predicted by Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA) to impact 237 categories of Biological Functions and Diseases ( Table S4A ). The top 10 categories included many aspects of NPC, such as hereditary neurological and developmental diseases, skeletal and muscular diseases, and metabolic diseases ( Figure 4H ). Next, we investigated whether the three miRNAs upregulated in NPC fibroblasts were altered in NPC fibroblast EVs. SEC was used to enrich EVs from conditioned media of each cell line and miRNA expression assayed. As expected, there were significantly fewer miRNAs expressed in EVs than in parent cells: of the 377 miRNAs screened, only 22 were sufficiently expressed and analysed ( Figure 4I , Table S3E ). The three miRNAs significantly upregulated in NPC fibroblast cells were not detectable in EVs. In fibroblast EVs, miR‐376a‐3p showed a two‐fold downregulation in NPC relative to CTL with p <0.05, though this result was not statistically significant based on FDR corrected thresholds ( Figure 4J ). We also sought to compare miRNA expression in fibroblast cells and fibroblast EVs to CSF EVs. Of the 187 miRNAs assayed, 34 were sufficiently expressed for group comparisons ( Figure 5A , Table S3F ). MiRNAs‐199a/b‐3p and ‐320a were significantly upregulated (FDR corrected threshold p < 0.015) by at least 1.5‐fold in NPC CSF EVs relative to CTL CSF EVs ( Figure 5B– C ). Two additional miRNAs (let‐7g‐5p and ‐885‐5p) were upregulated in NPC CSF EVs by at least 1.5‐fold with p < 0.05 but were not considered statistically significant based on the FDR ( Figure 5A , pink dots). To explore the potential impact of upregulated miR‐320a and ‐199a/b‐3p, which play known roles in cholesterol homeostasis (Lu et al. 2022b ; Aranda et al. 2022 ), we again used miRTarBase, TargetScan, and miRDB to identify 1,173 potential mRNA targets. By IPA, these targets were enriched in 154 categories of Biological Functions or Diseases ( Table S4B ). The top 10 categories included some overlap with predicted fibroblast pathways (e.g. gene expression and hereditary neurological disease), as well as unique pathways such as cell death and survival, organismal injury and abnormality, and hereditary psychological disorder ( Figure 5D ). Together, these results reveal five miRNAs that are significantly upregulated in NPC samples and implicated in pathways relevant to NPC1 function. Interestingly, there was no overlap in differentially expressed miRNAs between fibroblasts, fibroblast EVs, and CSF EVs, demonstrating the cell/tissue‐type specificity of EV miRNA expression. 3.5 Increased EV Concentrations in NPC Are Partially Attenuated by CD Treatment In the only study performed on human samples, Strauss et al. showed cells from an NPC1 patient fibroblast cell line released more EVs than a healthy CTL fibroblast (Strauss et al. 2010 ). However, other in vitro or in vivo models of NPC1 dysfunction have shown increased, decreased, or no change in EV concentration and size (Canfrán‐Duque et al. 2014 ; Albacete‐Albacete et al. 2020 ; Van Hoecke et al. 2021 ; Cashikar and Hanson 2019 ). We thus used single VFC to measure EV size and concentration in our larger cohort of patient samples. EVs were labeled with a membrane dye and a cocktail of PE‐conjugated antibodies against the three TS proteins CD63, CD81, and CD9. Ideal dilution and gating strategies for VFC were determined using ISEV recommendations ( Figures S2 –S 7 ) (Welsh et al. 2020 ). In both CSF and fibroblast conditioned medium, there were no significant differences in TS+ EV size between NPC and CTL groups ( Figure S11A, B ). However, there was a significant increase in the concentration of TS+ EVs in NPC CSF compared to CTL CSF ( Figure 6A ), which we observed was true across all five NPC samples rather than being driven by a specific NPC1 mutation ( Figure 6B ). Also, there was no significant difference in the concentration of total membranous particles present in NPC CSF versus CTL CSF ( Figure S11C ), suggesting this increase ( Figure 6B ) was specific to TS+ EVs in NPC patients. In fibroblasts, we observed much greater heterogeneity in TS+ EV concentrations from NPC cells relative to CTLs, demonstrated by a statistically significant increase in variance by F test ( p = 0.045) ( Figure 6C ). This effect was also trending towards significant ( p = 0.054) for total membranous particles released from fibroblasts ( Figure S11D ), suggesting that increased variance in EV release may be dependent on NPC1 mutation. When examining EV concentration by mutation, we found that the cell line with the lowest NPC1 expression (NPC‐F2) had the highest EV concentration ( Figure 6D ), and that there was a significant and inverse correlation between EV concentration and NPC1 expression ( Figure 6E ). Considering that this correlation was also true with TS+ EVs from CTL fibroblasts suggests the relationship between decreased NPC1 and increased EV release is not dependent on NPC disease conditions but may be due to a more fundamental cellular pathway. In comparing VFC data from CSF and fibroblasts we observed that the samples with the highest EV concentration (NPC‐C3 and NPC‐F2) shared the same genetic mutations (S733fsX10 and P434L) ( Table 1 , Figure 6B,D ). However, the overall pattern of EV concentration was not identical for CSF and fibroblasts, with mutations in NPC1 yielding a more uniform increase in CSF EVs ( Figure 6A ) compared to fibroblast EVs ( Figure 6C ). As NPC CSF donors were undergoing CD treatment at the time of CSF collection, we sought to investigate the CD treatment attenuates increased EV release in NPC. NPC‐F2 and CTL‐F2 fibroblast cell lines were treated with CD for 48 h and EV concentration and size were subsequently measured in the conditioned medium. In the untreated groups, the concentration of TS+ EVs was significantly increased in NPC‐F2 versus CTL‐F2 ( p = 0.039); while CD treatment of NPC‐F2 partially attenuated this increase to CTL‐F2 untreated levels ( p = 0.421) ( Figure 6F ). CD treatment in the NPC‐F2 but not CTL‐F2 cells also resulted in a small but significant increase in the size of total membranous particles but not the size of TS+ EVs ( Figure S12A,B ). Importantly, CD treatment did not affect the viability of either cell line ( Figure S12C ). Together, these data suggest that CD treatment modulates EV biogenesis in NPC. Further, it suggests that the elevated EV concentrations we observed in CSF from the NPC donors herein may be lessened and/or modulated by CD treatment. 3.6 NPC EVs Are Enriched in Endolysosomal Proteins Having observed that NPC samples have an increase in EVs positive for a pool of CD9, CD63, and/or CD81, we next investigated whether this change was generalized across the three populations or specific to certain EV subtypes. We captured then labeled CSF EVs using individual antibodies against CD9, CD63, and CD81 and used dSTORM imaging (ONI) to visualize EV subpopulations ( Figure 7A ). In human CSF, we identified single positive EVs expressing only one TS ( Figure 7B ), double positive EVs expressing two TS ( Figure 7C ), and triple positive EVs expressing all three TS ( Figure 7D ). In both CTL and NPC CSF, we found that CD9‐CD81 double positives constituted the largest EV population, followed by triple‐positives in CTL and CD9‐single positives in NPC ( Figure 7E ). The EV Profiling App on CODI (ONI) was used to quantify the size and biomarker distributions within the EV samples. Interestingly, the only statistically significant difference was a 2.6‐fold increase in CD63 single‐positive EVs in NPC CSF over CTL CSF ( Figure 7E ). In partial agreement with data published by Van Hoecke et al. ( 2021 ), there was a trending decrease in CD81‐CD9 positive EVs in NPC CSF ( Figure 7E ). We also observed the general pattern that all CD63‐positive populations increased in NPC CSF, while all CD81‐positive populations decreased (F igure 7E ). CD63, also known as lysosomal‐associated membrane protein 3 (Lamp3), is most commonly a maker of EVs that originate from the endolysosomal pathway (Palmulli et al. 2024 ; Mathieu et al. 2021 ). As endolysosomes are highly disrupted by NPC1 dysfunction, we next investigated whether NPC EVs were enriched in other endolysosomal markers. We used MBFC to measure the expression of 37 markers on EVs from NPC and CTL CSF samples, of which 32 were expressed ( Table S5A ). The only protein showing significant differential expression was lysosomal‐associated membrane protein 1 (Lamp1), which demonstrated a two‐fold increase in NPC CSF EVs relative to CTL CSF EVs ( Figure 8A ). Another protein in the same family, lysosomal‐associated protein 4 (Lamp4), had the largest fold‐change (> 5‐fold) in NPC over CTLs, but this change was not significant ( Table S5A ). We used VFC to further confirm significantly increased Lamp1+ EVs in pools of NPC CSF over CTL CSF ( Figure 8B ), which also demonstrated that Lamp1+ EVs in NPC were significantly smaller than CTLs ( Figure 8C ). We next examined the relative abundance of EVs enriched from media in the three CTL and five NPC fibroblast cell lines. Of the 37 EV markers assayed, 33 were expressed ( Table S5B ). Interestingly, we again observed an increase in LAMP1 ( Figure 8D ), as well as intercellular adhesion molecule‐1 (ICAM1) ( Figure 8E ). Further, in EVs from NPC fibroblasts the abundance of Lamp1+ and ICAM‐1+ EVs were positively correlated to each other ( Figure 8F ), and both inversely correlated with NPC1 expression ( Figure 8G , H ). Previous work has shown altered Lamp1 expression in tissues with disruptions in NPC1 (Wu et al. 2021 , Van Hoecke et al. 2021 , Cawley et al. 2020 ) However, we found that Lamp1 expression was not altered in fibroblast cells ( Figure 8I , J ), nor did Lamp1 cellular expression correlate with NPC1 cellular expression ( Figure 8K ). Together, these results suggest that loss of NPC1 is associated with an EV‐specific enrichment of Lamp1. 4 DISCUSSION These studies are the first to analyse the CSF EV profile in patients with mutations in NPC1 and a larger cohort of patient fibroblasts with NPC1 mutations. In our experiments, NPC CSF contained significantly higher EV concentrations than healthy CTL CSF, and EV concentrations in fibroblast conditioned medium were inversely correlated with NPC1 protein expression. Our results are in partial agreement with data showing increased EVs in NPC1 patient and mouse fibroblasts as well as NPC1 knockout oligodendrocyte and neuronal cell types (Strauss et al. 2010 ; Albacete‐Albacete et al. 2020 ; Guix et al. 2021 ); but in contrast with data on NPC1 rodent astrocyte and choroid plexus models, which showed decreased EVs (Wu et al. 2021 ; Van Hoecke et al. 2021 ) and with data from immortalized cell lines that show no change in EV concentration following NPC1 inhibition (Canfrán‐Duque et al. 2014 ; Cashikar and Hanson 2019 ). However, previous studies investigating the impact of NPC1 on EVs used a range of enrichment and measurement techniques, which can heavily influence results and may contribute to the disparate findings (Doyle and Wang 2019 ). Our VFC method was also based on the presence of a lipophilic dye that fluoresces after intercalating into lipid bilayers. (Soto‐Heulin et al. 2023 ) demonstrated that NPC1 EVs have an elevated lipid content compared to CTLs, including significant enrichment for hexosylceramide and lysophosphatidylcholine. It is thus possible that lipid‐based EV counting methods, such as our VFC pipeline, are biased by altered lipid enrichment in EVs from NPC1 mouse models. These considerations underline the challenges in measuring EV concentration and demonstrate the need to interpret results in their methodological context. While prior studies have investigated miRNA changes in an NPC1 patient fibroblast cell line and NPC1 knockout mouse spleen (Ozsait et al. 2010 ; Pergande et al. 2019 ), the miRNAs we identified as differentially expressed in NPC have not been previously associated with disease. We found that NPC CSF EVs show increased expression of miRs‐320a and ‐199a/b‐3p, as well as a trending increase in let‐7g‐5p and miR‐885‐5p compared to CTL CSF. Interestingly, miRs‐320a and ‐199a‐3p play known roles in cholesterol homeostasis (Lu et al. 2022b ; Aranda et al. 2022 ), and ‐885‐5p is elevated in patients with liver pathologies, which are also common to NPC (Gui et al. 2010 ). In fibroblast EVs only one miRNA, miR‐376a, showed a trending decrease in NPC EVs over CTL EVs. Although not previously linked to NPC, miR‐376a is dysregulated in other lipid disorders, including an upregulation in diseases marked by high levels circulating cholesterol in the serum (Pescador et al. 2013 ; Mangas et al. 2022 , Carvalho et al. 2021 ). Our data suggests the inverse may also be true: when cholesterol is sequestered in endolysosomes and unavailable to the rest of the cell, miR‐376a appears downregulated. We also observed no overlap in differentially expressed miRNAs between fibroblast cells, fibroblast EVs, and CSF EVs, in agreement with other groups demonstrating the specificity of EV miRNA packaging (Das et al. 2019 ; Dellar et al. 2022 ). It is also possible that the relationship between NPC1 and EVs is specific to tissue or cell type, especially given the unique impacts of NPC1 dysfunction on the CNS (Cariati et al. 2021 ). It is difficult to know where EVs in CSF come from, as by the time it is collected from the lumbar spine, CSF has come into contact with the ventricles, subarachnoid space, and arachnoid villi as well as the epithelial and endothelial cells lining the spinal column (Sandau et al. 2024 ). Any cell type in these regions could theoretically contribute EVs to CSF, and proteomics have shown that CSF EVs express neuronal, microglial, endothelial, and epithelial markers in relatively equal proportion (Guha et al. 2019 ). Further supporting this, our attempts to define the surface marker expression of CSF EVs using MBFC showed no clear trend in the expression of markers from any one tissue or cell type ( Table S5A ). One limitation to our study is that we do not know the NPC1 expression levels in CSF acquired from patients, as this information could add more clarity to our findings. It is possible that the five CSF patients all had similar, low levels of NPC1 protein expression, and that if the study was expanded to a more genetically diverse patient group, the CSF results would reflect the fibroblasts. That the S733fsX10/P434L mutant, which had near‐zero NPC1 expression, showed the highest EV concentration in both CSF and fibroblasts supports this hypothesis. Indeed, our discovery that NPC1 expression indirectly correlates with EV concentration may explain the disparate results obtained in previous studies, which utilized patient‐specific mutations (Strauss et al. 2010 ), genetic knockouts (Strauss et al. 2010 ; Van Hoecke et al. 2021 ), and the NPC1 inhibitor U18 (Canfrán‐Duque et al. 2014 ; Albacete‐Albacete et al. 2020 ; Wu et al. 2021 ; Guix et al. 2021 ; Cashikar et al. 2019 ). Each of these impacts NPC1 expression to a different extent; even studies that used U18 had different dosing strategies which could result in different amounts of inhibition, as has been demonstrated by U18 dose‐response curves (Moiz et al. 2025 ; Santos et al. 2015 ). Thus, dose‐response assays with U18 or NPC1 siRNA may be an effective way to measure the impact of NPC1 inhibition on EV concentration. Further, if performed in multiple cell types (e.g. fibroblasts, iPSC‐derived neurons), this could provide definitive, tissue‐specific information on the relationship between NPC1 expression and EV concentration. An additional limitation is that the NPC CSF donors were undergoing treatment with the experimental drug CD, making it difficult to determine whether results in the CSF cohort are driven by NPC1 pathology or CD treatment. However, none of our significant findings correlated to the amount of time NPC patients spent on CD (data not shown), suggesting the results are not CD‐driven. Previous studies in NPC1 knockout mice showed that CD treatment does not alter EV release, and CD does not alter EV cholesterol content in NPC1 knockout cell lines (Chen et al. 2010 ; Feltes et al. 2020 ). Regarding the increased concentration of EVs in NPC CSF, our parallel experiments in fibroblasts suggest that CD treatment may partially attenuate increased EV release observed in NPC1 mutant cells. However, to fully disentangle the effect of NPC1 and CD treatment on EVs, further experiments on CD‐treated and untreated NPC1 samples will be needed. Induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) neurons generated from NPC1 patient fibroblasts, which have been recently developed, could be an ideal tool for this question (Volkner et al. 2021 ; Burbulla et al. 2021 ). Our data suggests that perturbations to EVs in NPC are driven, at least in part, by perturbations of the endolysosomes. This was first evidenced by the increase in NPC CSF EVs that express only CD63, also known as Lamp3. CD63 is primarily expressed on endosomal membranes and has been shown to preferentially label endosome‐derived EVs (exosomes) (Palmulli et al. 2024 , Mathieu et al. 2021 ). Further evidence linking NPC1 dysfunction to endolysosomes was upregulation of Lamp1 on NPC CSF EVs, and trending increase in Lamp4 ( p = 0.092, Table S5A ). The Lamp proteins are localized to late endosomes and lysosomes, and Lamp1 has been found elevated in NPC1 rodent models (Wu et al. 2021 ; Van Hoecke et al. 2021 ; Cawley et al. 2020 ). Interestingly, a study in NPC patients found elevated Lamp1 in NPC cerebellar tissues, but no change in CSF Lamp1 (Cawley et al., 2020 ). This could indicate that increased Lamp1 in NPC CSF is specific to EVs. We observed a similar increase in Lamp1 expression in NPC fibroblasts EVs, but not NPC fibroblast cells. These findings may reflect specific packaging of Lamp1 into NPC1 EVs. However, Lamp1 may only be elevated in endolysosomes with altered NPC1 function and thus undetectable by immunoblotting whole cell lysate, as has been the case for other endolysosomal accumulations in NPC (Feltes et al. 2020 ). Our findings that NPC EVs are enriched in the Lamp proteins, and CD63 in particular, contribute to growing recognition of the role that CD63 and cholesterol play in EV biogenesis. Bonora et al. (2024) recently found that modulating cellular cholesterol directly impacts the release of endosomal EVs, and that greater cholesterol synthesis leads to greater CD63+ EV release. A possible explanation is provided by Palmulli et al. ( 2024 ), who demonstrated that CD63 sorts cholesterol into intraluminal vesicles for release as cholesterol‐rich, CD63‐positive exosomes. The relevance of this to disease was proven by Kestecher et al. ( 2024 ), who found significantly decreased concentrations of circulating CD63+ EVs in a mouse model of hypercholesterolemia, which causes elevated serum cholesterol but depleted endolysosomal cholesterol (Saint‐Pol and Fenart 2025 ). Our data suggests that the inverse is also true: when endolysosomal cholesterol is increased through NPC1 mutations, we observed significantly increased CD63+ EVs. One interpretation of these results is that increased release of Lamp‐positive EVs in NPC1 is a compensatory mechanism to remove endolysosomal content from over‐burdened cells. Further lipidomic studies on EV subpopulations in the context of NPC1 dysfunction would be illustrative. The compensatory hypothesis is further supported by the fact that inhibiting EV release in NPC1 loss of function cells exacerbates endolysosomal cholesterol accumulation (Lu et al. 2022a ), and conversely, that stimulating EV release in NPC1 models decreases endolysosomal cholesterol (Soto‐Huelin et al. 2023 ; Ilnytska et al. 2021 ). While removing toxic endolysosomal build‐up via exosomes may benefit the releasing cell, consequences for the recipient cell(s) are difficult to predict. If Lamp‐positive, cholesterol‐enriched exosomes enter recipient cells through endocytosis, they may exacerbate the cholesterol storage issues already present. However, exosomes taken up by alternative methods may be able to ameliorate the cholesterol starvation experienced at other cellular locations, such as the plasma membrane (Rosenbaum and Maxfield 2011 ). Thus, the increased NPC EVs we observed could have positive and/or negative consequences for disease pathology. Further investigations of EV uptake in NPC1 loss of function are needed. For instance, while our data suggests when cholesterol is sequestered in endolysosomes and unavailable to the rest of the cell, miR‐376a appears downregulated. However, to support the central premise of NPC1‐dependent regulation of miRNA content, further studies are needed. For instance, this would include establishing an NPC1 rescue experiment in NPC1‐mutant fibroblasts using wild‐type NPC1 expression, with functional confirmation of rescue (e.g. reduction of lysosomal cholesterol accumulation assessed by filipin staining). Studies to then assess whether the candidate miRNA signature, particularly within EV cargo, reverts toward control levels following NPC1 restoration. In addition, complementary NPC1 knockdown in control fibroblasts would further strengthen causal inference by demonstrating that loss of NPC1 function is sufficient to induce the observed miRNA changes. Together, these studies would support the central premise of NPC1‐dependent regulation of miRNA content. Ultimately, these studies were the first to analyse the profile of EVs in NPC patient CSF and a larger cohort of NPC patient fibroblasts. As is common for rare diseases, we were limited by a small number of patient samples which also displayed genetic and clinical heterogeneity. Also, as common for developmental disorders, our cohort was limited to studying NPC patients that were at least 17 years of age to age‐match with available healthy CTL participant samples. However, since NPC affects infants and children, we performed an exploratory study using CSF from NPC patients aged 2–32 years which revealed that younger age significantly correlated with Flotillin‐1 and CD81 protein levels in CSF ( Figure S1B,C ). These findings are in line with other studies that report correlations between age and EV protein in human CSF (Sandau et al. 2024 ; Tietje et al. 2014 ) and highlight the need for future studies in age‐matched cohorts to elucidate the impact of NPC1 mutations throughout development. Albeit our discoveries suggest a model that fits well with our data: loss of NPC1 drives cholesterol accumulation inside endolysosomes; this cholesterol is then sorted into intraluminal vesicles by CD63; these intraluminal vesicles are then released as exosomes that are enriched in endolysosomal markers. It seems likely that elements of this pathway are not unique to NPC, or even dependent on NPC1 loss, but are rather a result of endolysosomal cholesterol perturbations. With the context of the 2024 publications, our research also highlights the complexity of connecting cholesterol changes with EV changes: increased cellular cholesterol synthesis increases CD63+ EV release, but increased serum cholesterol decreases CD63+ EV release, and increasing cholesterol in endolysosomes (as in NPC) causes increased EV release. Thus, our discoveries contribute to a growing appreciation for the complex relationship between endolysosomal injury, cholesterol, and EVs, and provide new information about the fundamental cell biology behind a currently incurable childhood disease.
